intro.title:
Ticketing platform
Ticketmaster-style
intro.subtitle: A million people, fifty thousand seats, one narrow write path and one wide read path.

cues.cap: Designing a Ticketmaster-style ticketing platform, scenario by scenario.
The hard part is not volume but contention: a million people fighting over fifty thousand seats at 10:00 sharp. Let's follow the requests through the system.
cues.say: The hard part is not volume but contention: a million people fighting over fifty thousand seats at ten o'clock sharp. Let's follow the requests through the system.

steps.cap: The write path is narrow and strictly controlled: Waiting Room, API Gateway, Booking Service, with Redis for holds and Postgres as the source of truth.
steps.title: Write path
steps.note: Every hop is synchronous: the user waits for 201 PENDING. The gate at the edge lets through only what Postgres can absorb.

steps.cap: Everything after the booking is asynchronous: an Outbox Relay publishes to Kafka, and a Saga Orchestrator drives payment, ticket and notification.
steps.title: Async path
steps.note: The user does not wait for any of this. Each saga step retries on its own and has a compensation if the next one fails.

steps.cap: The read path is wide and fully separate: Seat Map Service, a Redis snapshot, WebSocket deltas and a CDN. Two hundred thousand refreshes per second never touch the seats table.
steps.title: Read path
steps.note: CQRS in practice: writes are strict, reads are eventually consistent and cheap. The seats table sees 0 of the 200 000 req/s.

scenes.title: From the waiting room to a paid ticket

steps.cap: At 10:00, five hundred thousand people press Buy in the same second. Every request hits the Waiting Room at the edge over HTTPS.
steps.say: At ten o'clock, five hundred thousand people press Buy in the same second. Every request hits the Waiting Room at the edge over H T T P S.
steps.code:
GET /events/123
→ 200 "You are #5432 in line"
steps.note: Nobody gets in yet. The waiting room holds everyone and shows a queue position.

steps.cap: Every few seconds it releases as many people as the database can handle, about 2 000 per second, each with a short-lived signed token. No valid token, no entry.
steps.say: Every few seconds it releases as many people as the database can handle, about two thousand per second, each with a short-lived signed token. No valid token, no entry.
steps.code:
token = sign({ pos: 5432, exp: now + 120 s })

no valid token → 429 Too Many Requests
steps.note: Backpressure point 1: the gate opens exactly as fast as Postgres can write.

steps.cap: The user picks seat 42 and clicks Reserve. The browser sends POST /bookings with the token and an Idempotency-Key; the gateway verifies the signature and calls Booking Service over gRPC.
steps.say: The user picks seat forty-two and clicks Reserve. The browser sends post slash bookings with the token and an idempotency key; the gateway verifies the signature and calls Booking Service over G R P C.
steps.code:
POST /bookings
Idempotency-Key: 7f3c…a1
{ event: 123, seat: 42 }

→ gRPC Booking.Create(event, seat, user)
steps.note: The same key on a retry returns the same booking, never a second one.

steps.cap: Booking Service first tries SET NX on a hold key in Redis with a ten-minute TTL. If the key already exists, someone else holds the seat and the answer is 'already taken' in under a millisecond, without touching the database.
steps.say: Booking Service first tries set N X on a hold key in Redis with a ten-minute T T L. If the key already exists, someone else holds the seat and the answer is already taken in under a millisecond, without touching the database.
steps.code:
SET hold:evt123:seat42 u42 NX EX 600
→ OK      we hold it
→ (nil)   someone else does, < 1 ms
steps.note: The lock is an optimization that stops 99.9% of the contention before Postgres. It is not the guarantee.

steps.cap: With the lock taken, it runs one SQL transaction: a conditional UPDATE that flips the seat to HELD only if it is still AVAILABLE, plus an INSERT into the outbox table.
steps.say: With the lock taken, it runs one S Q L transaction: a conditional update that flips the seat to held only if it is still available, plus an insert into the outbox table.
steps.note: Zero rows affected means someone won even with the lock, for example after a Redis failover. The database, not Redis, is the real guarantee.

steps.cap: On success the client gets 201 PENDING with ten minutes to pay. The seat is held, nothing is charged yet.
steps.say: On success the client gets two-oh-one pending with ten minutes to pay. The seat is held, nothing is charged yet.
steps.title: Booking Service → Client
steps.note: The request path ends here. Payment, ticket and email happen asynchronously.

steps.cap: Meanwhile the Outbox Relay reads the new outbox row, through a stream or CDC, and publishes BookingCreated to Kafka. Booking Service never writes to Kafka directly.
steps.say: Meanwhile the Outbox Relay reads the new outbox row, through a stream or C D C, and publishes Booking Created to Kafka. Booking Service never writes to Kafka directly.
steps.code:
SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL
→ produce booking-events
  { type: 'BookingCreated', booking: 'bk_981' }
→ UPDATE outbox SET published_at = NOW()
steps.note: Transactional outbox: the event is committed together with the booking, so it can never be lost or published without a booking.

steps.cap: The user enters the card and sends POST /bookings/bk_981/pay. The Saga Orchestrator, for example Temporal, consumes the event and runs the state machine: charge, issue ticket, notify.
steps.say: The user enters the card and sends post slash bookings slash pay. The Saga Orchestrator, for example Temporal, consumes the event and runs the state machine: charge, issue ticket, notify.
steps.code:
workflow bk_981:
  1. charge          (Payment Service)
  2. issue ticket    (Ticket Service)
  3. notify          (Notification Service)
  on failure → compensate
steps.note: Each step is a synchronous gRPC call with its own retries; the saga as a whole is asynchronous to the client.

steps.cap: Step one: the saga calls Payment Service over gRPC, which calls Stripe over HTTPS with an idempotency key, so a retried request can never charge the card twice.
steps.say: Step one: the saga calls Payment Service over G R P C, which calls Stripe over H T T P S with an idempotency key, so a retried request can never charge the card twice.
steps.code:
POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges
Idempotency-Key: bk_981-charge
amount = 12000, currency = 'eur'
→ 200 { status: 'succeeded' }

steps.cap: Steps two and three: Ticket Service generates the PDF with a QR code and stores it in object storage, and Notification Service sends the email.
steps.say: Steps two and three: Ticket Service generates the P D F with a Q R code and stores it in object storage, and Notification Service sends the email.
steps.code:
Ticket.Issue(bk_981)  → s3://tickets/bk_981.pdf
Notify.Send(user, 'ticket', { pdf })

steps.cap: Finally the saga marks the booking CONFIRMED and the seat BOOKED in Postgres and deletes the hold in Redis. The client learns over WebSocket that the ticket is issued.
steps.say: Finally the saga marks the booking confirmed and the seat booked in Postgres and deletes the hold in Redis. The client learns over websocket that the ticket is issued.
steps.title: Saga → Postgres, Redis, Client

scenes.title: Payment fails or the time runs out

steps.cap: The user closes the tab with a held seat. Nothing happens immediately: the Redis hold expires on its own after ten minutes, but the Postgres row still says HELD.
steps.say: The user closes the tab with a held seat. Nothing happens immediately: the Redis hold expires on its own after ten minutes, but the Postgres row still says held.
steps.title: Hold expired
steps.code:
TTL hold:evt123:seat42 → -2   (key is gone)

seats: status = 'HELD'
       hold_expires_at < NOW()
steps.note: Two mechanisms clean this up: a lazy check on the next attempt, and a periodic reaper.

steps.cap: The first mechanism is lazy: the next person who asks for seat 42 runs the same conditional UPDATE, and an expired hold counts as available right in the WHERE clause.
steps.say: The first mechanism is lazy: the next person who asks for seat forty-two runs the same conditional update, and an expired hold counts as available right in the where clause.
steps.title: Next client → Postgres
steps.code:
UPDATE seats SET status = 'HELD', held_by = $me
 WHERE seat_id = 42
   AND (status = 'AVAILABLE'
     OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < NOW()))
RETURNING seat_id;

steps.cap: The second mechanism is the Reaper Job: every thirty seconds, under a distributed lock, it returns expired holds to AVAILABLE so they show up in the seat map again.
steps.say: The second mechanism is the Reaper Job: every thirty seconds, under a distributed lock, it returns expired holds to available so they show up in the seat map again.

steps.cap: Now the other failure. The payment succeeds, but Ticket Service crashes. After N failed attempts the saga stops retrying and starts compensation.
steps.title: Saga: step 2 fails
steps.code:
1. charge        ✓  Stripe ch_8f2
2. issue ticket  ✕  retry 1, 2, … N
→ give up, run compensations

steps.cap: Compensation runs the saga backwards: a refund through Payment Service with a new idempotency key, release the seat in Postgres and Redis, and tell the user.
steps.title: Compensating actions

steps.cap: If the compensation fails too, the case goes to a dead-letter queue and a manual-intervention list. 'Paid, but no ticket' is an incident, not a retry.
steps.title: Compensation failed
steps.note: Alert on it: a DLQ that nobody reads is a silent data loss.

steps.cap: And a nightly reconciliation job compares our bookings with Stripe's settlement file and catches everything that slipped between the cracks.
steps.title: Nightly reconciliation
steps.code:
stripe settlement.csv  ⟷  bookings
bk_901 ✓   bk_902 ✓   bk_904 ✓
bk_903 paid, no ticket → ops queue
steps.note: Designed on the assumption that mismatches will happen; the question is how fast they are caught.

scenes.title: Watching the hall: 200 000 reads per second

steps.cap: While 2 000 people per second book, a million people watch the seat map and refresh it every five seconds. That is 200 000 requests per second, and none of them may reach the seats table.
steps.say: While two thousand people per second book, a million people watch the seat map and refresh it every five seconds. That is two hundred thousand requests per second, and none of them may reach the seats table.
steps.title: The read load
steps.code:
1 000 000 viewers / 5 s = 200 000 req/s
seats table:               0 req/s
steps.note: The read side is a separate system that only ever sees a snapshot.

steps.cap: Seat Map Service listens for changes, through a Kafka event or Postgres NOTIFY, and keeps a fresh snapshot of the whole hall in Redis.
steps.say: Seat Map Service listens for changes, through a Kafka event or Postgres notify, and keeps a fresh snapshot of the whole hall in Redis.
steps.code:
on SeatChanged { seat: 42, status: 'HELD' }:
  snapshot[42] = 'HELD'
  SET seatmap:evt123 <json>   -- whole hall

steps.cap: For the initial load the client fetches the map as JSON through the CDN, cached for one to two seconds. On a miss the edge pulls it once from Seat Map Service and serves everyone else from cache.
steps.say: For the initial load the client fetches the map as jason through the C D N, cached for one to two seconds. On a miss the edge pulls it once from Seat Map Service and serves everyone else from cache.
steps.code:
GET /events/123/seats
Cache-Control: max-age=2
→ CDN hit ratio ≈ 99 %, origin sees ~1 req/s per edge

steps.cap: Pages that are already open receive small delta messages over WebSocket: 'seat 42 is now taken', instead of the whole map.
steps.say: Pages that are already open receive small delta messages over websocket: seat forty-two is now taken, instead of the whole map.
steps.code:
WS → { seat: 42, status: 'HELD' }
WS → { seat: 17, status: 'AVAILABLE' }

steps.cap: The picture may lag by a second or two, so a click on a seat can still fail with 'just taken'. Reads are eventually consistent; writes are not.
steps.title: Stale reads are fine
steps.code:
click seat 42 → POST /bookings
→ 409 Conflict 'just taken'
→ pick another seat
steps.note: Reads: eventually consistent. Writes: strict, decided by the conditional UPDATE.

recap.title: What to say in the interview
recap.closing:
The lock is not correctness.
The database is.

items.text: Waiting room + token bucket = backpressure at the edge
items.cap: To sum up. A waiting room with a token bucket gives backpressure at the edge.

items.text: Redis SET NX hold = an optimization, not correctness
items.cap: A Redis hold with SET NX is an optimization, not correctness.
items.say: A Redis hold with set N X is an optimization, not correctness.

items.text: Conditional UPDATE + UNIQUE constraint = the guarantee
items.cap: A conditional UPDATE and a UNIQUE constraint are the real guarantee.
items.say: A conditional update and a unique constraint are the real guarantee.

items.text: Transactional outbox → Kafka → Saga with compensations
items.cap: A transactional outbox feeds Kafka, and a saga with compensations finishes payment, ticket and email.

items.text: Separate read path: Redis snapshot, WebSocket deltas, CDN
items.cap: And the seat map lives on a fully separate read path: Redis snapshot, WebSocket deltas and a CDN. The lock is not correctness. The database is.
